Inspired by Lakkaraju et al. (2017) on solving the evaluation problem when assessing algorithmic predictions in the presence of unobservables, commonly referred to as the selective labels problem, this paper examines the methodological challenges that arise when outcome data are only partially observed. The selective labels problem occurs when we only observe certain outcomes conditional on prior human decisions, creating a non-random sample that complicates model evaluation.
Consider the judicial system as an illustrative example. We observe whether a defendant fails to appear for their court date only if a human judge decides to release the defendant on bail. For defendants who are detained, we never observe what their behavior would have been had they been released. This selective labeling makes it considerably more difficult to evaluate predictive models, as the instances for which outcomes are observed do not represent a random sample of the population.
The selective labels problem extends naturally to the credit scoring domain. Financial institutions do not extend credit to a random sample of applicants and then passively observe repayment behavior. Rather, banks make deliberate decisions about whom to approve based on their assessment of creditworthiness. Banks want to lend to those who are likely to repay their loans. Consequently, observed default rates are conditional on the bank's approval decision, not representative of the underlying population of potential borrowers. This selection mechanism introduces systematic bias into any evaluation of predictive credit scoring models trained on historical lending data.
